title: Pride: Once Again a Protest
content:
By Inés M. Pousadela, Head of Research and Analysis

On the morning of 28 June, riot police sealed off Taksim Square with iron barriers and enforced bans on all weekend gatherings in Istanbul. Marchers pressed ahead anyway, re-emerging from side streets each time police dispersed them. By the end of the day police had detained at least 50 people, including a journalist. It was Istanbul Pride’s 24th edition, and the 12th year running that the authorities banned it outright.

title: Communities vs. Datacentres
content:
By Andrew Firmin, Editor-in-Chief

Few things unite Donald Trump’s most ardent supporters with the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, but datacentres are one of them. Across the USA, communities are joining forces across the political divide to oppose developments few want but governments seem determined to impose.

Michigan residents are among those who’ve come together across party lines to oppose plans for over a dozen datacentres. Polling shows just 28 per cent of the state’s population support the proposals. Local communities are fighting back, and similar struggles are unfolding across the world.

Read on Inter Press Service News

title: Guatemala: A Narrow Opening in a Captured Justice System
content:
By Inés M. Pousadela, Head of Research and Analysis

José Rubén Zamora, founder of elPeriódico, Guatemala’s now-defunct leading investigative newspaper, spent 1,295 days in detention before a court granted him house arrest on 12 February. He endured long stretches of solitary confinement in a military jail, held in near-constant darkness and subjected to treatment that six UN experts warned could amount to torture. His offence was simply doing his job. For decades, he exposed the corrupt dealings of Guatemala’s economic and political elites. Prosecutors are still trying to send him back to prison.

title: Choosing Courage over Despair: Civil Society Is Notching Up Wins Despite Hostile Conditions
content:
By Mandeep Tiwana, CIVICUS Secretary General

We live in a world where cruel and unaccountable power is on the ascendant. Powerful countries led by self-serving strongmen are wreaking havoc across borders in a neocolonial scramble for power and natural resources. Their disruption of the rules-based order through military action in breach of international law is leaving trails of death and destruction. Oligarchs powered by the entrenchment of market fundamentalism have come to monopolize large swaths of our economies. They are trying to influence how people think and act through their grip on the media, boosted by artificial intelligence (AI) and surveillance technology. These combined forces want civil society to believe nothing can stand in their way. But across the world, despite immensely challenging conditions, resistance is brewing and is notching up wins for peace, justice, equality, and environmental sustainability.

title: Art, Surveillance and the Politics of Memory
content:
By Deepthy Menon, Strategy and Narratives Facilitator, Urgent Action Fund Asia and Pacific

Across Southeast Asia, artists and cultural rights defenders are increasingly being cast as threats – to public morality, political order and dominant narratives about gender, sexuality, identity and belonging.

This is especially true for queer and trans artists, whose bodies, stories and performances often challenge the boundaries that states, religious authorities and conservative movements seek to impose. When their work is censored, surveilled or attacked, the consequences reach beyond artistic freedom. They touch the foundations of civic space: the right to speak, gather, remember, imagine and contest power.
